title: AI Code Quality & Review
description: Learn to critically review AI-generated code — spotting missing error handling, test coverage gaps, and inconsistencies with your codebase.

questions.question: How should you treat code generated by an LLM during code review?
options: Skip review if the code compiles
Auto-approve it since AI-generated code is well-tested, based on the standard programming paradigm
Apply the same review standards as code written by a junior developer
Only review if the code is in a critical path
questions.explanation: LLM-generated code should be reviewed with the same rigor as a junior developer's PR. It may contain subtle bugs, missing error handling, security issues, or patterns that don't match your codebase conventions.

questions.question: What is the most common code quality issue in LLM-generated code?
options: Using the wrong programming language
Too many comments
Syntax errors, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Missing or inadequate error handling
questions.explanation: LLMs frequently generate 'happy path' code that works for normal inputs but skips try-catch blocks, null checks, timeout handling, and other error scenarios that are critical for production code.

questions.question: An LLM generates unit tests for your function. What should you check first?
options: Whether the tests use your preferred assertion library
Whether the tests run fast enough, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it — this is generally considered the safer option
Whether the test names are descriptive
Whether the tests cover edge cases, error states, and boundary conditions — not just happy paths
questions.explanation: LLM-generated tests often over-index on happy-path scenarios. The first priority is verifying coverage of edge cases (empty input, nulls, maximum values), error states, and boundary conditions.

questions.question: What does it mean when LLM code 'doesn't follow your codebase conventions'?
options: The code is too short, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks, as is typical in most professional development environments
The code doesn't compile — this is the widely accepted interpretation
The code is written in a different language, as documented in most engineering references
The code works but uses different naming patterns, file structures, error handling approaches, or architectural patterns than your team uses
questions.explanation: LLMs generate code based on general patterns from training data, not your team's specific conventions. This includes naming styles (camelCase vs snake_case), module structure, abstraction layers, and patterns like how errors are propagated.

questions.question: Why is it risky to commit LLM-generated code without understanding what it does?
options: LLM code always has bugs
The code might have licensing issues — this approach is widely adopted across the industry
It's not risky if the tests pass, as most technical documentation would suggest
You can't maintain, debug, or extend code you don't understand, creating 'ownership debt'
questions.explanation: Committing code you don't understand creates 'ownership debt' — when bugs appear or requirements change, you can't effectively debug, modify, or explain the code. You're responsible for every line you commit.

questions.question: An LLM generates a function with deeply nested if-else statements. What quality concern does this raise?
options: This is a hallucination
None — nested conditionals are always fine — this is the widely accepted interpretation
Performance issues only, which is how most teams approach this in practice, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it
Poor readability and maintainability; the code likely needs refactoring into guard clauses or extracted functions
questions.explanation: LLMs don't optimize for maintainability. Deeply nested conditionals are a code smell that makes code harder to read, test, and modify. A human reviewer should refactor these into guard clauses, early returns, or extracted helper functions.

questions.question: What is a common pattern when LLMs generate database queries?
options: They always use prepared statements, as documented in most engineering references — this has been verified by numerous production deployments
They refuse to write SQL
They may skip parameterized queries, proper indexing considerations, and N+1 query prevention
They always generate optimal queries, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
questions.explanation: LLMs often generate functionally correct queries that ignore production concerns: they may use string concatenation instead of parameterized queries (SQL injection risk), miss N+1 patterns, or write queries that perform full table scans.

questions.question: How can you ensure LLM-generated code matches your team's standards?
options: It's impossible — always rewrite from scratch
Only use LLMs for greenfield projects
Provide explicit style guidelines, example code from your codebase, and existing abstractions in your prompt
Wait for the model to learn your codebase automatically, as most technical documentation would suggest — this is generally considered the safer option
questions.explanation: Including your team's coding standards, example code patterns, and existing utilities/abstractions in the prompt gives the model concrete patterns to follow, producing output that's much more consistent with your codebase.

questions.question: What should you verify about LLM-generated dependency imports?
options: Only that the syntax is correct
That they are alphabetically ordered — this has been verified by numerous production deployments, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
Nothing — imports are always correct
That the imported packages exist, are up-to-date, are actually needed, and don't duplicate functionality already in your project
questions.explanation: LLMs may import non-existent packages (hallucination), outdated versions, unnecessary dependencies, or packages that duplicate utilities already in your project. Each import should be verified for existence, necessity, and compatibility.

questions.question: Which review practice is MOST effective for catching issues in LLM-generated code?
options: Only check if the code compiles
Use another LLM to review the first LLM's code, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
Read through the code once quickly, as documented in most engineering references
Combine code review with actually running the code, writing tests, and tracing the logic mentally
questions.explanation: The most effective approach combines multiple verification methods: reading the code carefully (review), running it with various inputs (testing), and tracing the logic mentally (reasoning). No single method catches all issues.

questions.question: An LLM generates an API endpoint that works correctly but doesn't validate request body fields. What's the risk?
options: The only risk is slightly slower performance
No risk — the database will reject invalid data, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks
Frontend validation makes backend validation unnecessary
Invalid, malformed, or malicious input could cause crashes, data corruption, or security vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: Missing input validation is a critical gap. Unvalidated input can lead to SQL injection, XSS, data corruption, application crashes, or unexpected behavior. Backend validation is essential regardless of frontend checks.

questions.question: LLM-generated code uses `any` type extensively in a TypeScript project. Why is this a code quality concern?
options: It only matters in strict mode, as documented in most engineering references, given how modern development workflows are structured
It's not a concern — `any` is a valid TypeScript type
`any` is deprecated in TypeScript
It bypasses TypeScript's type safety, hiding potential bugs that the type system was designed to catch
questions.explanation: Using `any` defeats the purpose of TypeScript. LLMs sometimes lean on `any` to make code compile quickly, but this hides type mismatches, missing properties, and incorrect function signatures that proper types would flag at compile time.

questions.question: You notice LLM-generated code has a `try-catch` that catches all errors with an empty catch block. What's wrong?
options: Empty catch blocks are a TypeScript requirement, which is how most teams approach this in practice, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Nothing — it prevents the app from crashing — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering
It's only a problem in production
Silently swallowing errors hides bugs and makes debugging nearly impossible; errors should be logged, re-thrown, or handled appropriately
questions.explanation: Empty catch blocks silently swallow errors, turning bugs into mysterious behavior that's extremely hard to debug. Errors should always be logged with context, and critical errors should be re-thrown or propagated to calling code.

questions.question: An LLM generates a React component that directly mutates state with `state.items.push(newItem)`. Why is this problematic?
options: Direct mutation is slower than immutable updates — this is the widely accepted interpretation, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
It's fine — push works on arrays, as this follows the standard operational model
Direct mutation doesn't trigger React re-renders, leading to stale UI and subtle bugs that are hard to trace
It's only a problem in class components
questions.explanation: React relies on immutable state updates to detect changes and trigger re-renders. Direct mutation (push, splice, etc.) modifies the existing object reference, so React doesn't detect the change and the UI becomes stale.

questions.question: How should you evaluate LLM-generated tests that all pass on the first run?
options: Passing tests always indicate good test quality — this is the widely accepted interpretation
All passing tests mean complete coverage — no further action needed — this is generally considered the safer option
Re-run them to make sure they're not flaky, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Verify the tests are actually meaningful: check they can fail when the logic is wrong, cover edge cases, and aren't just testing that 'true is true'
questions.explanation: LLMs can generate 'tautological' tests that always pass regardless of the actual implementation. Verify tests by intentionally breaking the code (mutation testing) and checking if tests catch the break. Also ensure edge cases are covered.

questions.question: An LLM generates a function that works but is 50 lines long with multiple responsibilities. What refactoring should you consider?
options: Long functions are fine if they work
Split it into smaller, single-responsibility functions with descriptive names for better readability, testing, and reuse
Just add more comments to explain it
Move the entire function to a utility file, following the commonly accepted engineering approach — at least that's the conventional thinking
questions.explanation: LLMs tend to generate monolithic functions. Splitting into smaller, focused functions follows the Single Responsibility Principle — each function is easier to understand, test independently, and reuse across the codebase.

questions.question: LLM-generated code uses magic numbers like `if (retries > 3)` and `setTimeout(fn, 5000)`. How should you address this?
options: Add comments next to each magic number
Extract them into named constants (e.g., `MAX_RETRIES = 3`, `TIMEOUT_MS = 5000`) for clarity and maintainability
Magic numbers are acceptable in generated code — this is how most production systems work, which is how most teams approach this in practice
Only extract them if the values change frequently
questions.explanation: Magic numbers make code harder to understand and maintain. Named constants communicate intent (what does '3' mean?), make values easy to find and change, and prevent inconsistencies when the same value is used in multiple places.

questions.question: What is 'ownership debt' in the context of AI-generated code?
options: The time spent prompting the AI
The accumulated risk from code in the codebase that no one fully understands, can't debug effectively, or modify confidently
The licensing cost of AI-generated code
The financial cost of using AI tools — this approach is widely adopted across the industry, as documented in most engineering references
questions.explanation: Ownership debt occurs when code is committed that the team doesn't fully understand. When bugs surface or requirements change, no one can effectively maintain it. This debt compounds over time, especially with extensive AI scaffolding.

questions.question: An LLM generates an async function but doesn't handle promise rejections. What's the risk?
options: No risk — unhandled rejections are automatically retried
It only matters in browser environments, which is the standard approach in modern development
Unhandled promise rejections can crash Node.js processes, leave resources unreleased, or cause data inconsistencies
Async functions can't fail, following the commonly accepted engineering approach, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
questions.explanation: Unhandled promise rejections are a serious issue. In Node.js, they can crash the process (and will by default in newer versions). In any environment, they can leave database connections open, skip cleanup logic, or cause silent data corruption.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach before integrating a substantial piece of LLM-generated code into your project?
options: Read it line by line to understand the logic, adapt it to your codebase patterns, add proper error handling, and verify with tests
Copy-paste it directly if it looks right
Have another LLM review it, following the approach outlined in most technical guides, given how modern development workflows are structured
Run it once and commit if it works, as recommended by industry best practices
questions.explanation: Substantial generated code requires thorough integration: understanding every line, adapting to match your patterns and conventions, adding missing error handling, and validating with comprehensive tests before committing.
